verse.text: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the good news of God,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a person owned by another, not a hired servant. Paul's first readers in Rome, a city full of slaves and freed slaves, would have heard it that way. The Septuagint also uses the word for honoured figures such as Moses and David as ‘slaves of the Lord’, so it carries dignity as well as total belonging. Many translations soften it to ‘servant’; a growing number now print ‘slave’.

The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession, and the Septuagint uses the related verb for announcing God's saving reign. ‘Gospel’ once meant exactly this but is now heard mainly as a religious term or a kind of book. Most translations keep ‘gospel’ in Paul; several modern ones use ‘good news’.

verse.text: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy scriptures,
concerning his Son, who came from the seed of David according to the flesh,
who was appointed Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by resurrection from the dead: Jesus Christ our Lord,
verse.note: Elsewhere in the period the verb means to fix, determine or appoint, and that is how it is used in the rest of the New Testament. ‘Declared’ became traditional partly to avoid suggesting that Jesus only became God's Son at the resurrection. Most commentators now accept ‘appointed’ or ‘designated’, taking ‘in power’ with ‘Son of God’: the one who was already Son was installed as Son-in-power by the resurrection.

verse.text: through whom we received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles for the sake of his name,
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean the obedience that springs from faith, the obedience that consists in faith, or simply faithful obedience. The literal rendering is kept because the Greek does not decide between them and scholars remain divided. The same phrase returns at the close of the letter (16:26).

Greek has one word here for ‘nations’ and ‘Gentiles’; in the plural it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. ‘Among all the nations’ is therefore equally possible in this verse. ‘Gentiles’ is used because Paul goes on to describe his mission as directed to non-Jews (verse 13).

verse.text: and among them you also are called to belong to Jesus Christ.
To all who are in Rome, loved by God, called to be holy ones: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The word is the ordinary adjective ‘holy’ used as a noun for all members of the community, as people set apart for God; it echoes the Septuagint's language for Israel. ‘Saints’ now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue, which is not what is meant. Many translations keep ‘saints’; others use ‘God's holy people’.

verse.text: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed throughout the whole world.
For God, whom I serve with my spirit in the good news of his Son, is my witness how unceasingly I make mention of you
always in my prayers, asking that somehow, now at last, by God’s will, the way may be opened for me to come to you.
For I long to see you, so that I may share with you some spiritual gift to strengthen you;
that is, to be encouraged together among you through each other’s faith, yours and mine.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, that I have often planned to come to you, and have been prevented until now, so that I might have some fruit among you also, just as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verse.note: The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of siblings or fellow members, and Paul's letters were read aloud to congregations that included women (several are greeted by name in chapter 16). ‘Brothers’ alone now sounds as if only men are addressed. Older translations have ‘brethren’ or ‘brothers’; many recent ones have ‘brothers and sisters’.

verse.text: To Greeks and to barbarians, to the wise and to the foolish, I am a debtor;
verse.note: In Greek usage the word meant anyone who did not speak Greek or share Greek culture; it could be condescending but did not in itself mean ‘savage’. ‘Greeks and barbarians’ was a stock way of saying all humanity as seen from the Greek side, just as ‘Jew and Greek’ in verse 16 is the same division seen from the Jewish side.

verse.text: so for my part I am eager to proclaim the good news to you also who are in Rome.
For I am not ashamed of the good news, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: “But the righteous one will live by faith.”
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify. The phrase itself is disputed: it may mean God's own rightness shown in acting to save and set things right, as often in the Psalms and Isaiah, or a right standing that comes from God as a gift. ‘Righteousness’ is kept as the traditional and majority rendering; some scholars prefer ‘justice’ or ‘covenant faithfulness’. ‘Unrighteousness’ in verses 18 and 29 is the negative of the same word.

The phrase is compressed and disputed. It may be an emphatic way of saying ‘by faith from start to finish’, or it may mean from God's faithfulness to human faith, since the Greek word covers both faith and faithfulness. ‘By faith’ in the quotation that follows (Habakkuk 2:4) is the same Greek phrase as ‘from faith’ here. The quotation can also be read as ‘the one who is righteous by faith will live’.

verse.text: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth in unrighteousness,
because what can be known about God is plain among them, for God has made it plain to them.

For ever since the creation of the world his unseen qualities, his eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood through the things he has made, so that they are without excuse,
because although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasonings, and their senseless heart was darkened.
Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
and exchanged the glory of the imperishable God for the likeness of an image of a perishable human being, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.
Therefore God handed them over in the desires of their hearts to impurity, to the dishonouring of their bodies among themselves.
They exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and worshipped and served the creation rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.
For this reason God handed them over to dishonourable passions. For their females exchanged natural relations for those contrary to nature,
verse.note: Paul does not use the ordinary words for ‘women’ and ‘men’ in verses 26–27 but ‘females’ and ‘males’, the terms of the Greek version of Genesis 1:27 (‘male and female he made them’). The choice fits a passage that argues from creation, and the rendering keeps it visible. Most translations have ‘women’ and ‘men’.

verse.text: and likewise the males also, abandoning natural relations with the female, were inflamed with craving for one another, males committing shameful acts with males and receiving in themselves the repayment that was due for their error.
And just as they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God handed them over to an unfit mind, to do what is not proper,

note.traditional: reprobate mind / debased mind / depraved mind

verse.note: Paul plays on two related words: they did not ‘approve’ God after testing, so God gave them over to a mind that ‘fails the test’. ‘See fit’ and ‘unfit’ reproduce the echo. The traditional renderings give the sense of a mind that has failed but lose the wordplay.

verse.text: filled as they are with every kind of unrighteousness, wickedness, greed and malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit and spite. They are gossips,
slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents,
verse.note: In earlier Greek the word is passive, ‘hated by the gods’, and some scholars read it so here (‘hateful to God’). Because every other item in the list is a vice and not a consequence, most translators take it actively, as here.

verse.text: senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.
Though they know full well God’s righteous decree, that those who practise such things deserve death, they not only do them but also approve of those who practise them.
verse.note: This translation normally renders the word ‘righteous requirement’ or ‘righteous act’. Here it refers not to something God requires but to his verdict that such conduct deserves death, so ‘decree’ is used. ‘Righteous’ is retained to show the link with ‘righteousness’ in verse 17.

verse.text: Therefore you have no excuse, whoever you are, you who judge; for in judging the other person you condemn yourself, because you who judge practice the very same things.
verse.note: The Greek is literally ‘O human being’, a stock form of address to an imagined listener in the ancient debating style known as diatribe. It names no one in particular and is not specific to men, which ‘whoever you are’ conveys. Many scholars think the listener is already the Jewish critic of Gentile vice addressed by name in verse 17; others take it as any moralist at all.

verse.text: Now we know that the judgment of God falls, in accordance with truth, on those who practice such things.
And do you suppose, whoever you are, you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?
Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not knowing that God's kindness is leading you toward turning back?
verse.note: ‘Repentance’ now suggests mainly feeling sorry. The Greek word, shaped by the prophets' call to ‘return’ to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct; ‘will not turn back’ in verse 5 is the negative of the same word. Most translations keep ‘repentance’ as an established term understood to include a change of life.

verse.text: But in keeping with your hardness and your heart that will not turn back, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God,
who will repay each person according to their works:

note.term: who will repay each person according to their works

verse.note: The wording echoes Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, and readers who knew the Scriptures would have recognised it. How this judgment according to works fits with Paul's later argument about being justified apart from works of the law is a long-standing debate; the text here states it without qualification.

verse.text: to those who by perseverance in good work seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life;
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for ‘age’. In Jewish usage ‘eternal life’ is the life of the age to come, so the phrase speaks of a kind of life as well as its unending length. ‘Eternal’ is the standard rendering; a minority of translators prefer ‘life of the age to come’.

verse.text: but for those who act from selfish ambition and disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, there will be wrath and fury,
verse.note: The word is rare before the New Testament, where it is used of self-interested pursuit of office. Older translations linked it with a similar-sounding word for strife and rendered ‘contentious’; most lexicons now prefer ‘selfish ambition’ or ‘self-seeking’, though the matter is not settled.

verse.text: affliction and distress, upon every human being who does evil, the Jew first and also the Greek;
but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
For there is no favoritism with God.
For all who sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who sinned under the law will be judged by the law.
For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God; rather, the doers of the law will be justified.
verse.note: ‘Righteous’ and ‘justified’ in this verse, ‘just judgment’ in verse 5, ‘unrighteousness’ in verse 8 and ‘righteous requirements’ in verse 26 all belong to one Greek word-family, which English splits between ‘right’ words and ‘just’ words. ‘Justified’ here means declared to be in the right at God's judgment. Some scholars prefer ‘justice’ language throughout, as translations into most other languages do.

verse.text: For whenever Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, they, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves.
verse.note: The Greek word means ‘peoples’ or ‘nations’, and in the plural, in Jewish usage, the non-Jewish peoples. English uses ‘Gentiles’ or ‘nations’ according to sense, but it is one word in Greek, here and in the quotation in verse 24.

The phrase can be attached to what follows, as here (they do by nature what the law requires), or to what precedes: Gentiles ‘who do not have the law by nature’, that is, by birth. The first is the majority reading and usually takes these to be Gentiles in general acting on a moral sense. The second is favoured by those who think Paul means Gentile believers, in whom the law is written on the heart as Jeremiah 31:33 promises.

verse.text: They show the work of the law written on their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness and their thoughts, one against another, accuse or even defend them,
on the day when God judges the hidden things of people, according to my good news, through Christ Jesus.
verse.note: ‘Gospel’ has become a religious term and a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between ‘gospel’ and ‘good news’.

verse.text: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God
and know his will and discern what matters, being instructed from the law,
and are confident that you yourself are a guide to the blind, a light to those in darkness,
a corrector of the foolish, a teacher of the immature, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
you, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?
You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you rob temples?
verse.note: The verb's ordinary meaning is to plunder temples, and here it most naturally refers to profiting from the property of pagan shrines, perhaps by trading in goods taken from them, despite professing to abhor idols. Some take it more broadly as ‘commit sacrilege’, including withholding what is owed to the Jerusalem temple. What actual practice Paul has in mind is uncertain.

verse.text: You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by breaking the law?
For, just as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

note.term: blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you

verse.note: Paul quotes Isaiah 52:5 in its ancient Greek version, which includes the words ‘because of you’ and ‘among the Gentiles’; the Hebrew text is shorter. In Isaiah the nations mock God's name because of Israel's exile; Paul applies the line to dishonour brought on God by lawbreaking.

verse.text: Circumcision is indeed of benefit if you practice the law; but if you are a lawbreaker, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.
So if the uncircumcised man keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?
And the man who is uncircumcised by nature but carries out the law will judge you, who, with the written code and circumcision, are a lawbreaker.
For the Jew is not the one who is so in plain view, nor is circumcision what is in plain view, in the flesh;
rather, the Jew is the one who is so in what is hidden, and circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not the written code. Such a person's praise comes not from people but from God.

note.term: by the Spirit, not the written code
note.traditional: in the spirit, not in the letter

verse.note: The Greek has simply ‘in spirit, not letter’. It can mean an inward, spiritual circumcision as against a literal one, or circumcision carried out by God's Spirit as against the written law; Paul's similar contrasts in Romans 7:6 and 2 Corinthians 3:6 favour the second, and most recent commentators adopt it. ‘Letter’ means the law as a written text, as in verse 27, not the modern contrast between the letter and the spirit of a rule.

In Hebrew the name Judah, from which ‘Jew’ derives, is linked with the verb ‘to praise’ (Genesis 29:35; 49:8). Many scholars see a play on that link here: the one who truly bears the name receives praise from God. The pun does not work in Greek, so how many of Paul's first readers would have caught it is uncertain.

verse.text: What advantage, then, does the Jew have, or what is the benefit of circumcision?
Much in every way. First of all, they were entrusted with the oracles of God.
What then? If some were unfaithful, will their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God?
verse.note: The verb can mean either 'refused to believe' or 'proved unfaithful'. Verses 2–3 play on one word-family in Greek: Israel was 'entrusted' with God's words, some were 'unfaithful', and their 'unfaithfulness' cannot cancel God's 'faithfulness'. The rendering keeps that chain visible, but 'did not believe' is an equally possible reading, and many translations adopt it.

verse.text: Absolutely not! Let God be true, though every person be a liar, as it is written: “So that you may be vindicated in your words and prevail when you are judged.”
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous/just, righteousness/justice, and justify all translate related Greek words. Here, where God is the one shown to be in the right, 'vindicated' is the natural English. Elsewhere in the chapter the same verb is 'justify' and the noun is 'righteousness', and in verse 26 'just' and 'justifies' are used so that the Greek wordplay can be heard. Some scholars prefer 'justice' for the noun throughout.

The quotation is from Psalm 51:4 in its Greek form. The Greek verb can be read as passive ('when you are judged') or as middle ('when you go to law' or 'when you judge'). The Hebrew text of the psalm has 'when you judge'. The passive is followed here because it suits Paul's picture of God being put on trial and winning.

verse.text: But if our unrighteousness shows the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust when he inflicts wrath? I am speaking in a human way.
Absolutely not! Otherwise how will God judge the world?
But if through my lie the truth of God abounds to his glory, why am I still being judged as a sinner?
And why not say, as we are slanderously reported to say and as some claim we say, “Let us do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is deserved.
What then? Are we any better off? Not at all, for we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin,
verse.note: The meaning of this one-word question is disputed. It may mean 'Do we (Jews) have an advantage?', which is the majority reading followed here, or 'Are we at a disadvantage?', or 'Are we making excuses?' The reply can also be read as 'Not entirely' instead of 'Not at all'.

verse.text: as it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one;

note.term: There is no one righteous, not even one

verse.note: Verses 10–18 are a chain of Scripture quotations joined into a single indictment, a technique known from other Jewish writings of the period. The lines are drawn, in their Greek form, mainly from Psalm 14:1–3 (paralleled in Psalm 53), Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3, Psalm 10:7, Isaiah 59:7–8 and Psalm 36:1. They are presented here as one quotation, as Paul presents them.

text.q: there is no one who understands, there is no one who seeks God.
All have turned aside, together they have become worthless; there is no one who does good, there is not even one.
Their throat is an open grave, with their tongues they deceive, the venom of asps is under their lips;
their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.
Their feet are swift to shed blood,
ruin and misery are in their ways,
and the way of peace they have not known.
There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

verse.text: Now we know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those within the law, so that every mouth may be silenced and the whole world become answerable to God,
because by works of the law no flesh will be justified before him; for through the law comes knowledge of sin.
verse.note: The phrase means things done because the law of Moses requires them. Scholars dispute its focus. The traditional reading takes it as any effort to gain standing with God by obedience. Many recent interpreters think Paul has chiefly in view the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws and sabbath. The translation leaves the phrase open.

verse.text: But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been disclosed, attested by the Law and the Prophets,
verse.note: The Greek can mean God's own righteousness, that is, his faithful action to set things right, or a righteous standing that comes from God to people. Both readings have strong support, and some hold that Paul intends both. The literal phrase is kept so that the reader can weigh them.

verse.text: the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. For there is no distinction,
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'faith of Jesus Christ' and can be read two ways: the believer's faith in Christ, or Christ's own faithfulness, meaning his obedience to the point of death. 'Faith in Jesus Christ' is the traditional and still majority reading, but 'the faithfulness of Jesus Christ' has substantial scholarly support. On that reading the following phrase, 'for all who believe', is not a repetition.

verse.text: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
and they are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus,
whom God put forward as a place of atonement, through faith, by his blood. This was to demonstrate his righteousness, because he had passed over the sins committed beforehand
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word is the name of the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Hebrews 9:5 uses it in the same way. The rendering lets that allusion be heard. Whether Paul means the ark cover itself ('mercy seat'), a sacrifice that turns away wrath ('propitiation') or one that removes sin ('expiation') is a long-running dispute.

verse.text: in the forbearance of God; it was to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the one who justifies the person who has faith in Jesus.
verse.note: The Greek is literally 'the one who is of the faith of Jesus'. As in verse 22, this can mean the person who has faith in Jesus, which is the majority reading, or the person who lives from the faithfulness of Jesus. The grammar allows both.

verse.text: Where, then, is boasting? It is shut out. By what kind of law? A law of works? No, but by a law of faith.
verse.note: Paul uses the same word, 'law', that he has used for the law of Moses. Some take it here in a looser sense, 'principle' or 'rule': boasting is excluded on the principle of faith. Others think he still means the Mosaic law, viewed as calling for faith and not for works. 'Law' is kept so that the play on the word remains visible.

verse.text: For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it refers to all the peoples other than Israel. English translations render the same word 'Gentiles' or 'nations' according to context. Paul's argument in the next verse rests on Israel's daily confession that God is one (Deuteronomy 6:4): if there is one God, he is God of all peoples.

verse.text: since God is one, and he will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.
Do we then nullify the law through this faith? Absolutely not! On the contrary, we uphold the law.
What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?

note.traditional: What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?

verse.note: The sentence can be punctuated differently: 'What then shall we say? Have we found Abraham to be our forefather according to the flesh?', which would make the question about whether Abraham's fatherhood is merely a matter of physical descent. The manuscripts also vary in where they place 'found', and a few omit it. The rendering here follows the majority of translations and commentators.

verse.text: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about—but not before God.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'justify', 'justification', 'righteous' and 'righteousness' in this chapter all translate forms of the same root. To justify someone is to declare or set them in the right, and the reader should hear the link with 'righteousness' in verse 3. Translations into most other languages use one word for 'justice' throughout, and some scholars prefer 'justice' in English as well.

verse.text: For what does the scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”
verse.note: The verb is an ordinary bookkeeping term for entering something to a person's account, which is why Paul can move straight to wages and debt in verse 4. The quotation is Genesis 15:6 in its Greek form, and the same verb recurs in the psalm quoted in verses 7–8 (Psalm 32:1–2). It is rendered 'count' throughout the chapter so that the eleven occurrences can be heard as one word.

verse.text: Now when someone works, the wages are not counted as a matter of grace but as a matter of debt.
verse.note: In everyday Greek the word meant a favour freely given, and many modern versions translate 'as a gift' here. 'Grace' is kept because Paul uses the identical phrase again in verse 16, and the argument depends on the reader hearing the two together.

verse.text: But when someone does not work but believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, that person’s faith is counted as righteousness,
verse.note: To a reader who knew the Scriptures this phrase was startling. In the Greek Old Testament acquitting the ungodly is what a corrupt judge does, and it is forbidden (Exodus 23:7; Proverbs 17:15; Isaiah 5:23). Paul deliberately describes God in the terms of that prohibition.

verse.text: just as David also pronounces the blessing on the person to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:

text.q: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered;
blessed is the man whose sin the Lord will never count against him.”

verse.text: Is this blessing, then, on the circumcised, or on the uncircumcised as well? For we say, “Faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.”
How then was it counted? When he was circumcised or when he was uncircumcised? Not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised.

And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he would be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them,
and the father of the circumcised, for those who are not only circumcised but also follow in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.

note.term: not only circumcised but also follow
note.traditional: not only circumcised but who also walk in the footsteps

verse.note: The Greek repeats the article before 'follow', which strictly would describe two groups: the circumcised, and also those who follow Abraham's faith. Most interpreters judge that the argument requires one group, circumcised people who also share Abraham's faith, and treat the extra article as loose grammar or an early slip. The rendering here follows that view.

verse.text: For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring, that he would be heir of the world, did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.
verse.note: Genesis promises Abraham a particular land and many descendants; it never says in so many words that he would inherit the world. By Paul's time Jewish interpretation had widened the land promise to take in the whole earth, and Paul assumes that reading.

verse.text: For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise nullified.
For the law brings about wrath; but where there is no law, there is no transgression either.

This is why it is by faith, so that it may be a matter of grace, so that the promise may be guaranteed to all the offspring—not only to those who are of the law but also to those who are of the faith of Abraham, who is the father of us all,

as it is written, “I have made you a father of many nations.” He is our father in the sight of the God in whom he believed, who gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were.
verse.note: The Greek word translated 'nations' here, quoting Genesis 17:5, is the same word translated 'Gentiles' elsewhere in Romans (for example 3:29). Paul's point depends on this: the scripture that made Abraham father of many nations is, to a Greek ear, also making him father of many Gentiles.

note.term: calls things that are not as though they were
note.traditional: calleth those things which be not as though they were

verse.note: The phrase can mean that God summons non-existent things into existence, the language of creation, as several modern versions translate it. It can also mean that God speaks of things that do not yet exist, such as Abraham's descendants, as if they already did. The rendering here keeps the Greek wording, which allows both.

verse.text: Against hope, in hope, he believed, so that he became the father of many nations, according to what had been said: “So shall your offspring be.”
And without weakening in faith he considered his own body, as good as dead since he was about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah’s womb;

note.traditional: he considered not his own body

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read 'he did not consider his own body'. The earliest witnesses lack the negative, and that is the text translated here: Abraham looked squarely at the facts and still believed. Either reading makes the same overall point.

verse.text: yet with regard to God’s promise he did not waver through lack of faith, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God
and being fully convinced that what God had promised he was also able to do.
That is why “it was counted to him as righteousness.”
But the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone,
but also for ours. It is going to be counted to us who believe in the one who raised from the dead Jesus our Lord,
who was handed over for our trespasses and raised for our justification.

note.traditional: delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification

verse.note: The same Greek preposition stands in both halves of the verse, and 'for' is used twice to keep the parallel. In the first half it means 'because of'. In the second it is usually taken as 'with a view to' our justification, though some read 'because of' there too. 'Handed over' echoes the Greek of Isaiah 53:12, where the servant is handed over because of the people's sins.

verse.text: Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
verse.note: Many early and important manuscripts read 'let us have peace' (a difference of one vowel, which sounded alike when the letter was read aloud). The edition translated here, with most modern editors and translations, reads the statement 'we have peace', which suits the argument: Paul is describing what follows from justification, not urging it.

Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'justify', 'justification', 'righteous' and 'righteousness' in this chapter all translate forms of the same root. The verb means to declare or set someone in the right, as a court does. Translations from Latin and most other languages use their one word for 'justice' throughout, and some scholars prefer 'justice' in English as well.

verse.text: through whom we have also gained access by faith into this grace in which we stand; and we boast in the hope of the glory of God.
verse.note: The same verb occurs in verses 2, 3 and 11, and its ordinary meaning is to boast or take pride in something. Many English versions soften it to 'rejoice' or 'exult'; others have 'boast'. 'Boast' is kept here because Paul has just excluded boasting in one's own standing (3:27; 4:2) and now names what believers may rightly boast in. The form could also be read as 'let us boast'.

verse.text: And not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance,
endurance produces tested character, and tested character produces hope.
And hope does not put us to shame, because God's love has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean God's love for us or our love for God. Most interpreters take it as God's love for us, since verses 6–8 go on to describe how God has shown that love. A minority, following Augustine, read it as love for God.

verse.text: For while we were still weak, Christ died at the right time for the ungodly.
For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person, though for a good person perhaps someone might even dare to die.
But God demonstrates his own love for us in this: while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more, then, having now been justified by his blood, we will be saved through him from the wrath.
verse.note: The Greek says simply 'the wrath'. Many translations add 'of God' for clarity, and that is certainly whose wrath is meant: the coming judgment on wrongdoing that Paul has described in 1:18 and 2:5. The text is left as Paul wrote it.

verse.text: For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we will be saved by his life.
And not only that, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
Therefore, just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin, and so death spread to all people, because all sinned—
verse.note: Paul begins a comparison ('just as...') and breaks off without completing it, turning aside in verses 13–17 to explain and qualify it. The comparison is restarted and finished in verse 18 ('so also...'). The dash at the end of the verse marks the break.

The Greek connecting phrase is brief and much debated. Most modern scholars take it as 'because'. The old Latin translation rendered it 'in whom', that is, in Adam, a reading that was influential in Western teaching on original sin but is now generally thought not to fit the Greek. Some scholars propose 'with the result that all sinned'.

verse.text: for until the law sin was in the world, but sin is not charged to anyone's account when there is no law.
Yet death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of the transgression of Adam, who is a pattern of the one who was to come.
verse.note: The word meant a mould, model or pattern. Many versions keep 'type', which is a technical term of later theology and no longer clear English, while some others also have 'pattern'. Paul's point is that Adam, as one man whose act affected all, corresponds in advance to Christ, though the following verses stress how unlike the two are.

verse.text: But the gracious gift is not like the trespass. For if by the trespass of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound to the many.
verse.note: The Greek noun is formed from the word for 'grace' and means something given as an act of favour. 'Free gift' is the usual rendering; 'gracious gift' is used so that the link with 'grace' later in the verse can be heard. Paul uses two other, more ordinary words for 'gift' in verses 15–17, which are rendered simply 'gift'.

'The many' is a Semitic way of speaking of the whole mass of people as contrasted with the one; it does not mean 'many but not all'. The same group is called 'all people' in verses 12 and 18. How far Paul means the second 'all' and 'the many' to extend is debated, since verse 17 speaks of 'those who receive' the gift.

verse.text: And the gift is not like what came through the one who sinned. For the judgment following one trespass led to condemnation, but the gracious gift following many trespasses led to justification.
verse.note: This Greek noun usually means a righteous requirement or a righteous act, and it is rendered 'righteous act' in verse 18. Here it stands as the opposite of 'condemnation', and nearly all interpreters take it to mean the verdict that sets someone in the right. Paul probably chose this form instead of his usual word for justification (used in verse 18) because its ending matches the Greek words for 'judgment' and 'condemnation'.

verse.text: For if by the trespass of the one death reigned through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ.
So then, as through one trespass condemnation came to all people, so also through one righteous act justification that brings life came to all people.
verse.note: The Greek can equally be read 'the trespass of one... the righteous act of one', since 'one' may refer to the person and not to the deed. Either way the reference is to Adam's disobedience and to Christ's obedience, usually understood as his death. The sentence has no verb in Greek; 'came' is supplied.

verse.text: For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.
Now the law came in alongside so that the trespass might increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,
so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness, leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering; a minority of translators render 'life of the age to come'.

verse.text: What then shall we say? Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?
Certainly not! We who died to sin, how can we still live in it?
Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
So we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with the likeness of his death, we will certainly also be united with that of his resurrection.

note.term: united with the likeness of his death
note.traditional: united with him in the likeness of his death

verse.note: The Greek adjective means 'grown together, joined'. Many translations supply 'with him' and take 'the likeness of his death' as the manner of the union. The Greek has no 'with him', and the rendering here takes 'the likeness' as the thing believers are joined to; both readings are grammatically possible. The second half of the verse is compressed in Greek ('but also of the resurrection') and 'united with that of' is supplied from the first half.

verse.text: We know this: our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, and we might no longer be slaves to sin.
verse.note: The verb means to make something ineffective or put it out of operation, and can extend to abolishing it altogether. Older versions have 'destroyed'; the rendering here keeps the commoner sense, that the body as sin's possession loses its hold, without implying the physical body is annihilated.

verse.text: For the one who has died has been justified from sin.
verse.note: Most English versions render 'freed' or 'set free' here, but the verb is Paul's ordinary word for 'justify' (declare in the right, acquit), from the same word-family as 'righteousness' later in the chapter. A different verb for 'set free' appears in verses 18 and 22. The sense is probably that death settles sin's legal claim on a person; many scholars think Paul is adapting a general maxim that death clears all debts. That it amounts to release from sin's power is a fair inference, which is why the traditional rendering exists.

verse.text: Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him,
since we know that Christ, raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer has mastery over him.
For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.
In the same way, you too must count yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
So do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey the body's desires,

and do not go on presenting the parts of your body to sin as weapons of unrighteousness. Instead, present yourselves to God as people alive from the dead, and the parts of your body to God as weapons of righteousness.
verse.note: The traditional 'instruments' is possible, since the word can mean a tool, but its usual sense is 'weapon', and it clearly means that elsewhere in Paul's letters (Romans 13:12; 2 Corinthians 6:7; 10:4). The military picture fits the context, with sin 'reigning' in verse 12 and paying a soldier's 'wages' in verse 23. Many commentators prefer 'weapons', though most English versions keep 'instruments'.

verse.text: For sin will not have mastery over you, since you are not under law but under grace.
What then? Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? Certainly not!
Do you not know that if you present yourselves to someone as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one you obey, whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?
But thanks be to God that you, who were slaves of sin, obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over,

note.term: to which you were handed over

verse.note: Some older versions reverse the construction so that the teaching is delivered to the believers. The Greek says the believers were handed over to the teaching, which fits the chapter's picture of slaves transferred from one master to another. The verb is also the usual one for passing on tradition, and Paul may intend that echo.

verse.text: and that, set free from sin, you were enslaved to righteousness.

I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, leading to more lawlessness, so now present the parts of your body as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.
For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.
So what fruit did you have then from the things you are now ashamed of? For the end of those things is death.

note.term: from the things you are now ashamed of

verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and the sentence can be divided differently: 'So what fruit did you have then? Things of which you are now ashamed.' On that reading Paul answers his own question; on the reading adopted here the implied answer is 'none'. Editors and translators are divided.

verse.text: But now, set free from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit, leading to holiness, and the end is eternal life.
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for 'age'. In Jewish usage 'eternal life' is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as an unending one. 'Eternal' is the standard rendering and is kept; a minority of translators render 'life of the age to come'.

verse.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verse.note: The word was used especially for a soldier's pay or ration-money, continuing the military picture of verse 13. Sin pays out what has been earned. The contrasting word, 'gift', is related to 'grace' and denotes something given freely, not earned.

verse.text: Or do you not know, brothers and sisters (for I am speaking to people who know the law), that the law rules over a person for as long as that person lives?
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole Roman community. 'Brothers' alone would suggest to a modern reader that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep 'brothers' with a footnote.

verse.text: For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he lives; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.

So then, while her husband lives she will be called an adulteress if she becomes another man’s; but if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress when she becomes another man’s.

So, my brothers and sisters, you too were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might become another’s, his who was raised from the dead, in order that we might bear fruit for God.
For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions that came through the law were at work in our members to bear fruit for death.
verse.note: 'Flesh' in Paul often means more than the physical body: it is human existence in its weakness and its orientation away from God. 'When we were in the flesh' describes a former condition of life, not simply being alive in a body. Some translations paraphrase it as 'sinful nature', but the traditional word is kept here because Paul's contrast with 'Spirit' depends on it.

verse.text: But now we have been released from the law, having died to what held us fast, so that we serve as slaves in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary one for doing a slave's service and picks up the slavery language of the previous chapter (6:16–22). 'Serve' alone loses that connection. Most translations have 'serve'; a few have 'are slaves' or similar.

note.term: in the newness of the Spirit
note.traditional: in newness of spirit / in the new way of the Spirit

verse.note: Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so the word may be God's Spirit or the human spirit. Most interpreters take it as the Holy Spirit, anticipating chapter 8, and that reading is followed here. 'The letter' means the law as a written code.

verse.text: What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! Yet I would not have known sin except through the law. For I would not have known coveting if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”

note.term: I would not have known sin

verse.note: Who the 'I' of verses 7–25 is has been debated since antiquity. It may be Paul's own experience, a representative voice for Adam, for Israel under the law, or for humanity generally. It is also disputed whether verses 14–25, in the present tense, describe life before or after coming to Christ. The translation leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

Paul quotes the opening of the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21) without its list of objects. The Greek noun here and in verse 8 comes from the same root as the verb in the commandment, so 'coveting' and 'covet' keep the link visible. The word covers wrongful desire of any kind, not only sexual desire, which 'lust' now suggests.

verse.text: But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of coveting. For apart from law sin is dead.
I was once alive apart from law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life,
and I died, and the very commandment that was meant for life was found, in my case, to lead to death.
For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.
So then, the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: 'righteous' and 'just', 'righteousness' and 'justice', come from the same root. Older English versions have 'just' here. The sense is that the commandment is in the right and requires what is right.

verse.text: Did what is good, then, become death for me? Certainly not! Rather, it was sin, so that it might be shown to be sin, producing death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.
For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am made of flesh, sold under sin.
verse.note: The image is of the slave market: a person sold passes into the power of the buyer. Sin is pictured as the owner, continuing the slavery language of chapter 6. Some translations spell this out as 'sold as a slave to sin'.

verse.text: For I do not understand what I carry out. For I do not practice what I want; instead, what I hate is what I do.
But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.
But as it is, it is no longer I who carry it out, but sin that lives in me.
For I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh. For the wanting lies close at hand for me, but carrying out the good does not.
For I do not do the good that I want; instead, the evil that I do not want is what I practice.
But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who carry it out, but sin that lives in me.
So I find this law: when I want to do good, evil lies close at hand for me.
verse.note: Most interpreters take 'law' here in a looser sense, a rule or regular pattern, and many translations say 'principle'. Others hold that Paul still means the law of Moses: 'I find, as regards the law, that when I want to do good, evil lies close at hand.' 'Law' is kept so that the reader can see Paul using one word throughout verses 21–25.

verse.text: For I delight in the law of God in my inner self,
but I see a different law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.
What a wretched person I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?

note.traditional: the body of this death / this body of death

verse.note: In the Greek, 'this' can attach either to 'body' or to 'death', giving 'the body of this death', as in older versions. The difference is small. Either way the phrase means the body as the place where sin and death hold sway.

verse.text: Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself with my mind serve the law of God as a slave, but with my flesh the law of sin.
verse.note: Manuscripts differ here: some read 'Thanks be to God', others 'I thank God', the reading behind the King James Version. Still others have 'the grace of God', which turns the phrase into an answer to the question in verse 24. Most modern editions prefer 'Thanks be to God', and the sense is little affected.

verse.text: So there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

note.term: those who are in Christ Jesus
note.traditional: who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit (added in the King James Version)

verse.note: Later manuscripts add “who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” at the end of this verse. The earliest witnesses lack the words, and they are generally thought to have been copied in from verse 4.

verse.text: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and death.
verse.note: The “you” is singular. Many manuscripts read “me”, which continues the first-person voice of chapter 7, and a few read “us”. The evidence is closely divided; the edition translated here reads “you”.

verse.text: For what the law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did: sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as a sin offering, he condemned sin in the flesh,
verse.note: In Paul “flesh” often means more than the physical body. Here and through verse 13 it is human nature in its weakness and its bent away from God, treated almost as a power that people can live “in” or “according to”. The traditional word is kept because the contrast with “Spirit” depends on it.

The Greek is literally “concerning sin”. In the Greek Old Testament this phrase is the regular term for the sin offering, and many scholars think Paul's readers would have heard it that way. Others take it more generally, “to deal with sin”; the question remains disputed.

verse.text: so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.

note.traditional: righteous requirement; righteousness of the law

verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify). “Righteous requirement” here, “righteousness” in verse 10 and “justified” in verses 30 and 33 all translate related Greek words, a connection English cannot show.

verse.text: For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.
For the mindset of the flesh is death, but the mindset of the Spirit is life and peace,
because the mindset of the flesh is hostility toward God: it does not submit to God’s law, nor indeed can it.
And those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.
But if Christ is in you, then though the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness.

note.traditional: the Spirit is life; your spirit is alive

verse.note: The Greek word can be the human spirit or God's Spirit, and it is not marked either way. Some translations read “your spirit is alive”, in contrast with the body. Since Paul writes “is life”, not “is alive”, and the Spirit gives life in verses 2 and 11, many scholars take it as the Spirit of God, as here.

verse.text: And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in you.

note.term: because of his Spirit who dwells in you
note.traditional: through his Spirit who dwells in you

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two forms that differ only in grammatical case. One means “because of his Spirit”, the reading of the edition translated here; the other means “through his Spirit”, which most English versions follow. Both are ancient and well attested, and either way the indwelling Spirit is the pledge of resurrection.

verse.text: So then, brothers and sisters, we are debtors, but not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh;
for if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.
verse.note: Paul's word is “sons”, which here includes women and men alike; in verses 16, 17 and 21 he switches to the neutral “children”. “Sons” is kept because it ties believers to “his own Son” (verses 3, 29, 32) and to “adoption” (verses 15, 23), a word built on “son” that denoted the legal adoption of an heir. Some modern versions use “children” throughout.

verse.text: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery, leading back into fear; rather, you received the Spirit of adoption, in whom we cry out, “Abba, Father!”
verse.note: Abba is Aramaic for “father”, the address Jesus used in prayer (Mark 14:36). Paul keeps the Aramaic word and puts the Greek for “Father” beside it, which suggests the cry was known in that form even in Greek-speaking congregations.

verse.text: The Spirit himself testifies with our spirit that we are children of God.
And if children, then heirs too: heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.
For I consider that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed to us.
For the creation in eager expectation awaits the revealing of the sons of God.
For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly but because of the one who subjected it, in hope
verse.note: Paul does not name who subjected creation. Most interpreters understand God, with reference to the curse on the ground in Genesis 3, since only God could subject it “in hope”. A minority think of Adam, whose disobedience brought the curse.

verse.text: that the creation itself will also be set free from its slavery to decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together and suffering birth pains together until now.
And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, also groan within ourselves as we await adoption, the redemption of our bodies.
For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what they see?
But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with endurance.
In the same way, the Spirit also helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes with wordless groans,
and he who searches hearts knows what the mindset of the Spirit is, because he intercedes for the holy ones in accordance with God’s will.
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. Other translations use “God's people” or keep “saints”.

verse.text: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.

note.term: all things work together for good
note.traditional: all things work together for good

verse.note: The Greek can also be read with God as the unstated subject: “he works all things together for good” or “in all things he works for good”. Some early manuscripts add “God” to make that explicit. The rendering here takes “all things” as the subject, which is the simplest reading of the shorter text.

verse.text: For those he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he would be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.
And those he predestined he also called; and those he called he also justified; and those he justified he also glorified.
What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?
He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also, with him, freely give us all things?
Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? It is God who justifies.
verse.note: Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, so the replies in verses 33 and 34 can be read as statements, as here, or as further rhetorical questions: “Will God, who justifies? Will Christ, who died?” The sense is much the same either way, since no accuser or judge is left to stand against those God has vindicated.

verse.text: Who is the one to condemn? It is Christ who died, or rather, who was raised, who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.
Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or sword?
As it is written, “For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we were considered sheep for slaughter.”
No, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us.
For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor rulers, neither things present nor things to come, nor powers,
neither height nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
I am speaking the truth in Christ, I am not lying, and my conscience bears witness with me in the Holy Spirit,
that I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.
For I could wish that I myself were accursed, cut off from Christ, for the sake of my brothers and sisters, my kin according to the flesh.
verse.note: In the Septuagint this word names something handed over to God for destruction and so removed from ordinary use. Paul says he would accept that fate, separated from Christ, if it could benefit his fellow Israelites; many readers hear an echo of Moses' offer in Exodus 32:32. The verb rendered 'I could wish' can also mean 'pray', and its tense marks the wish as one that cannot actually be carried out.

verse.text: They are Israelites; theirs are the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the giving of the law, the worship, and the promises.
Theirs are the fathers, and from them, according to the flesh, comes the Christ, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen.

note.term: who is over all, God blessed forever
note.traditional: who is over all, God blessed for ever

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts had no punctuation, and the sentence can be divided in two ways. As rendered here, following the punctuation of the SBLGNT, the words describe Christ and call him God. The alternative puts a full stop after 'the Christ' (or after 'over all') and reads the rest as a separate blessing: 'God who is over all be blessed forever.' The grammar is often judged to favour the first reading, but the question remains disputed, partly because Paul seldom if ever calls Christ 'God' so directly elsewhere.

verse.text: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel,
nor are they all children because they are Abraham’s offspring; rather, “It is through Isaac that your offspring will be called.”
verse.note: The Greek word is literally 'seed', a singular noun used collectively for descendants. 'Offspring' keeps the collective singular without the archaic sound of 'seed'; it is used for the same word in verses 8 and 29. The verb 'called' in this quotation from Genesis 21:12 is the same one Paul uses for God's calling in verses 12 and 24 to 26.

verse.text: That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as offspring.
For this word was one of promise: “About this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.”
And not only that, but there is also Rebecca, who conceived by one man, our father Isaac.
For when they were not yet born and had done nothing good or bad, so that God’s purpose in choosing might stand,

note.traditional: the purpose of God according to election

verse.note: The Greek noun means a choice or selection. The traditional 'election' is accurate as a technical term, but in modern English it suggests voting. Most scholars agree that the phrase describes a purpose of God that operates by his own choice, which is what the rendering here expresses.

verse.text: not by works but by the one who calls, it was said to her, “The older will serve the younger.”
As it is written: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
verse.note: The quotation is Malachi 1:2-3, where Jacob and Esau stand for the nations Israel and Edom. In biblical idiom 'love' and 'hate' set side by side often express preference for one over another, not emotional hostility (compare Genesis 29:30-31 and Luke 14:26). How far that softens the statement here is debated; the plain word is kept in the text.

verse.text: What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not!
For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomever I have compassion.”
So then, it depends not on the one who wants or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.
For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might display my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”
So then, he has mercy on whom he wants, and he hardens whom he wants.
You will say to me then, “Why then does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?”
But who are you, O human being, to answer back to God? Will what is formed say to the one who formed it, “Why did you make me like this?”
Or does the potter not have the right over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?
But what if God, wanting to display his wrath and make known his power, bore with great patience vessels of wrath made ready for destruction,
verse.note: The Greek participle leaves the logical connection open. It may mean 'because he wanted' to display his wrath, so that the patience served that display. Or it may mean 'although he wanted' to, so that the patience held it back. The rendering keeps the Greek's openness. The sentence in verses 22 to 24 is also unfinished in Greek, an 'if' with no conclusion, which is why it is rendered 'what if'.

The Greek form can be passive ('made ready', without saying by whom) or middle ('having made themselves ready'). Paul uses a different and explicitly active verb for the vessels of mercy, 'which he prepared beforehand'. Some interpreters take the contrast as deliberate; others hold that God is the implied agent in both cases. The rendering leaves the agent unstated, as the Greek does.

verse.text: and did so to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory—
us, whom he also called, not only from among Jews but also from among Gentiles?
verse.note: The Greek word means 'peoples' or 'nations'. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it refers to the non-Jewish peoples, for which English uses 'Gentiles'. It is the same word that is translated 'nations' elsewhere in the New Testament.

verse.text: As he also says in Hosea: “I will call those who are not my people ‘my people,’ and her who is not beloved ‘beloved’;

text.q: and it will be that in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”

verse.text: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: “Though the number of the sons of Israel be like the sand of the sea, the remnant will be saved;

text.q: for the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.”

note.term: completing it and cutting it short
note.traditional: For he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth

verse.note: Many later manuscripts have a longer form of this verse, closer to the Greek of Isaiah 10:22-23, and the King James Version follows it. The earliest witnesses have the shorter text translated here. The Greek is compressed and its sense is uncertain: 'word' may mean God's sentence or reckoning, and the two participles may describe carrying it out completely and swiftly.

verse.text: And as Isaiah said beforehand: “If the Lord of Hosts had not left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.”
verse.note: Paul's Greek, following the Septuagint of Isaiah 1:9, leaves the Hebrew word tseva'ot untranslated as 'Sabaoth'. It means 'armies' or 'hosts', and the title presents God as commander of the heavenly armies. It is translated here because 'Sabaoth' is easily mistaken for 'Sabbath'.

verse.text: What then shall we say? That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness, the righteousness that is by faith;
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. The 'injustice' denied of God in verse 14 is the negative of the same word. 'Righteousness' is kept here for being in the right before God; some scholars prefer 'justice' or 'covenant faithfulness'.

verse.text: but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not reach that law.
Why? Because they pursued it not by faith but as if by works. They stumbled over the stumbling stone,
as it is written: “Look, I am laying in Zion a stumbling stone and a rock that makes people fall, and the one who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

note.term: a rock that makes people fall

verse.note: The Greek word refers to something that trips a person up or traps them. 'Offence' now suggests hurt feelings, which is not the meaning. The quotation combines Isaiah 28:16 with a phrase from Isaiah 8:14, so that the foundation stone God lays in Zion is also the stone people stumble over.

The Greek pronoun can mean 'him' or 'it', that is, the stone. Paul quotes the line again at 10:11 with clear reference to Christ, so most interpreters take the stone here as Christ, and the rendering follows them. The verb is from the same word-family as 'faith' in verses 30 and 32 and could also be translated 'trusts'.

verse.text: Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God for them is for their salvation.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul’s congregations included both. Older translations have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent ones render it as here.

verse.text: For I bear witness for them that they have zeal for God, but not in accordance with knowledge.
For, not knowing the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.

note.traditional: the righteousness of God; God’s righteousness

verse.note: The phrase can mean the right standing that God gives, God’s own uprightness, or God’s action to set things right; the Greek does not decide, and scholars are divided. The contrast with “their own” suggests a standing that comes from God, but the other senses are not excluded. Greek has one word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify), so the same word could be rendered “justice”.

verse.text: For Christ is the end of the law, so that there may be righteousness for everyone who believes.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean a termination or a goal and outcome. Some interpreters hold that Christ brings the law’s role to a close, others that he is what the law was aiming at, and many that both are intended. “End” is kept because the English word can carry both senses.

verse.text: For Moses writes that the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it.

note.term: the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it
note.traditional: Moses writes about the righteousness that is based on the law, that the person who does these things will live by them

verse.note: Manuscripts differ over where the word “that” stands and over the wording that follows. The reading translated here, adopted by SBLGNT, makes the sentence a paraphrase; the other reading gives a nearly direct quotation of Leviticus 18:5. On either reading Leviticus 18:5 is the passage in view.

verse.text: But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks like this: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will go up into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)

note.term: Do not say in your heart

verse.note: Verses 6 to 8 adapt Deuteronomy 30:12–14, with an opening phrase from Deuteronomy 9:4. There Moses says that God’s commandment is not far off in heaven or beyond the sea but near at hand. Paul gives the words to a personified “righteousness that comes from faith”, applies each line to Christ, and has “the abyss” where Deuteronomy has the sea.

verse.text: or, “Who will go down into the abyss?” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).
But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
because if you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
verse.note: The verb means to acknowledge or state something openly, often in a public or binding setting. “Confess” is the traditional rendering and is still used by most translations, but in current English it mainly suggests admitting guilt, which is not in view here. Some modern versions likewise use “declare” or “acknowledge”.

note.traditional: that Jesus is Lord; the Lord Jesus

verse.note: The Greek is simply “Lord Jesus” as the object of the verb. Most interpreters take it as the content of the declaration, “Jesus is Lord”, which appears elsewhere in Paul as an early Christian acclamation. Some older translations render it “confess the Lord Jesus”.

verse.text: For it is with the heart that one believes, leading to righteousness, and with the mouth that one declares, leading to salvation.
For the scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”
For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, since the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call on him.
For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
verse.note: The quotation is from Joel 2:32 (3:5 in the Greek version), where “the Lord” stands for the personal name of Israel’s God. The surrounding verses, with “Jesus is Lord” and “the same Lord is Lord of all”, indicate that Paul applies the line to Jesus. Most interpreters read it this way.

verse.text: How, then, are they to call on one in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in one they have not heard? And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming?

note.traditional: of whom they have not heard

verse.note: The Greek construction normally means hearing a person speak, not hearing about a person. On that reading Christ himself is heard in the proclamation of those who are sent. Many translations keep “of whom they have not heard”, which is possible; many commentators prefer the direct sense adopted here.

verse.text: And how are they to proclaim unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things!”
But not all obeyed the good news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what they heard from us?”
verse.note: The noun belongs to the same word-family as “bring good news” in the line from Isaiah just quoted in verse 15, and Paul is drawing on that link. “Gospel” is the standard rendering and means the same thing, but it hides the connection.

note.traditional: our report; our message (and in verse 17, “faith comes by hearing”)

verse.note: The Greek noun can mean either the act of hearing or the thing heard, a report. Isaiah’s line uses it in the second sense, and Paul repeats the same word twice in verse 17 to draw his conclusion. Most translations have “message” or “report” here and “hearing” in verse 17; one rendering is kept for both so that the reasoning can be followed.

verse.text: So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “the word of God”, which older English versions follow; the earliest witnesses have “of Christ”. The phrase may mean the message about Christ or the word Christ himself speaks; the Greek allows either.

verse.text: But I ask, did they not hear? Indeed they did: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world.”

note.term: Their voice has gone out into all the earth

verse.note: The words are from Psalm 19:4 (18:5 in the Greek version), where the voice is that of the heavens declaring God’s glory. Paul borrows them for the spread of the proclamation. Interpreters disagree on whether he means this as proof from Scripture or as a deliberately sweeping way of saying the message has gone out widely.

verse.text: But I ask, did Israel not know? First Moses says, “I will make you jealous over what is no nation; over a nation without understanding I will make you angry.”

note.traditional: those who are not a nation; them that are no people

verse.note: The quotation is from Deuteronomy 32:21. “Nation” here is the same Greek word that in the plural is usually rendered “Gentiles”. Paul hears in the Song of Moses an anticipation of non-Jewish peoples coming to Israel’s God and of Israel being provoked by it.

verse.text: And Isaiah is bold enough to say, “I was found by those who were not seeking me; I showed myself to those who were not asking for me.”
But about Israel he says, “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and defiant people.”
I ask, then: has God rejected his people? Absolutely not! For I too am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.
God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what the scripture says in the passage about Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?
verse.note: The Greek says simply ‘in Elijah’. Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a section of Scripture was commonly cited by its subject. The passage is 1 Kings 19:10–18.

text.q: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.”

verse.text: But what does the divine reply say to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal.”
So in the same way, at the present time too, there has come to be a remnant by a choice of grace.
verse.note: The Greek noun is the ordinary word for a selection or choice. ‘Election’ is the traditional rendering and remains standard in theological writing, but in modern English it suggests voting. In verse 7 the same word is used concretely for the people chosen (‘the chosen’), and it returns in verse 28.

verse.text: And if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

note.term: otherwise grace would no longer be grace

verse.note: Many later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, add: ‘But if it is by works, it is no longer grace; otherwise work is no longer work.’ Most of the earliest witnesses lack the sentence, and most scholars regard it as a later expansion. SBLGNT omits it.

verse.text: What then? What Israel is seeking, it did not obtain. The chosen obtained it, but the rest were hardened,
as it is written: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, to this very day.”
And David says: “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;

text.q: let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and keep their backs bent always.”

verse.text: I ask, then: did they stumble so as to fall? Absolutely not! Rather, by their misstep salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous.
verse.note: The Greek word means ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it is the regular term for the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it ‘Gentiles’ in that sense and ‘nations’ where peoples as such are meant; both represent one Greek word.
