The word denotes a lapse or wrongdoing and is usually rendered ‘trespass’ or ‘transgression’. Paul sets it here beside ‘stumble’ and ‘fall’, and ‘misstep’ keeps both the moral sense and the image. It refers to Israel's failure to accept the good news, not to a trivial slip.

verse.text: Now if their misstep means riches for the world, and their defeat riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their fullness mean!
verse.note: The word means what fills or completes something. Here and in verse 25 many interpreters take it numerically (‘their full number’, ‘full inclusion’), in contrast with the present remnant. Others take it as Israel's complete restoration. ‘Fullness’ leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch, then, as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I honor my ministry,
in the hope that I may somehow make my own flesh and blood jealous and save some of them.
For if their being cast aside means reconciliation for the world, what will their being taken back mean, if not life from the dead?

note.traditional: their rejection / the casting away of them

verse.note: Most interpreters understand this as God's temporary setting aside of unbelieving Israel, matched by ‘their being taken back’. A minority read it as Israel's own rejection of the good news. The Greek word differs from the one for ‘rejected’ in verses 1–2, where Paul denies that God has rejected his people.

verse.text: If the firstfruits are holy, so is the whole batch of dough; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verse.note: The image comes from Numbers 15:17–21, where the first portion of each batch of dough is offered to God. Paul's point is that the consecrated part marks the whole as God's. Whether the firstfruits and the root stand for the patriarchs or for the present remnant of Jewish believers is debated; most take the root to be the patriarchs.

verse.text: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, though a wild olive, were grafted in among them and came to share in the rich root of the olive tree,
do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, it is not you who carry the root, but the root that carries you.
You will say, then, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.”
True enough: they were broken off for lack of faith, and you stand by faith. Do not think highly of yourself, but be afraid.
For if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.
Consider, then, the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but God's kindness toward you, if you continue in his kindness; otherwise you too will be cut off.
And they too, if they do not continue in their lack of faith, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.

For if you were cut out of what is by nature a wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!
verse.note: Normal practice was to graft shoots from a cultivated olive onto wild stock, not the reverse. Paul's own phrase shows that he knows his picture runs against ordinary procedure. The point is that the inclusion of Gentiles is God's doing and not the natural course of things.

verse.text: For I do not want you to be unaware of this mystery, brothers and sisters, so that you will not be wise in your own eyes: a hardening has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in,
and in this way all Israel will be saved, as it is written: “The deliverer will come from Zion; he will turn ungodliness away from Jacob.

note.term: and in this way all Israel will be saved
note.traditional: and so all Israel shall be saved

verse.note: The Greek adverb normally expresses manner (‘in this way’) and not time (‘and then’), though some interpreters argue for a temporal sense. ‘All Israel’ is also disputed. Most scholars take it as the Jewish people as a whole, not necessarily every individual; others take it as the total of chosen Jews across history, and a minority as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile together.

text.q: And this is my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.”

verse.text: As regards the good news, they are enemies for your sake; but as regards the choice, they are beloved for the sake of the forefathers.
verse.note: ‘Gospel’ has become a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations already alternate between ‘good news’ and ‘gospel’.

verse.text: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
For just as you were once disobedient to God but have now been shown mercy through their disobedience,
so they too have now been disobedient, so that by the mercy shown to you they too may now be shown mercy.

note.term: by the mercy shown to you
note.traditional: by the mercy shown to you

verse.note: In Greek this phrase stands before ‘so that’ and could be read with what precedes: ‘they have been disobedient for the sake of the mercy shown to you’. Most translators and commentators take it with what follows, as here, matching the structure of verse 30. Some manuscripts also lack the second ‘now’ in this verse.

verse.text: For God has confined all in disobedience so that he may show mercy to all.
O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how untraceable his ways!
For “who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?”

text.q: “Or who has given to him first, that he should be repaid?”

verse.text: For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.
So I urge you, brothers and sisters, through the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a sacrifice, living, holy, pleasing to God, which is your rational worship.
verse.note: The adjective was common in the philosophy of the period for what belongs to reason or befits a rational being, and moralists used it to contrast thoughtful devotion with the mere slaughter of animals. Many translations render it 'spiritual', and some 'true and proper'; 'rational' stays closer to ordinary usage and fits the 'renewing of your mind' in the next verse. The noun covers the service of worship, especially sacrificial worship.

verse.text: And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is: what is good and pleasing and perfect.
verse.note: The Greek word is a term of time, not place. Paul shares the Jewish framework of two ages, the present one and the one to come, and tells his readers not to take their shape from the present one. 'World' is the traditional rendering and several modern versions keep it, though others also use 'age'.

verse.text: For through the grace given to me I say to every one of you: do not think of yourself more highly than you ought to think, but think so as to think sensibly, each according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned.
verse.note: This may mean a quantity of faith that God gives in differing amounts to different believers, or a measuring standard, namely the faith all believers share, by which each is to assess himself. Both readings have scholarly support. The translation keeps the traditional wording, which leaves the question open.

verse.text: For just as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function,
so we, the many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.
We have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;

note.traditional: Having gifts ... let us use them

verse.note: Verses 6 to 8 in Greek are a single clipped sentence with no main verb: 'having gifts ... if prophecy, in proportion to faith; if service, in the service', and so on. Most translations supply an instruction such as 'let us use them', and the context supports hearing the list as exhortation. The translation keeps the Greek's compressed form and does not add the words.

note.traditional: according to the proportion of faith

verse.note: The Greek has 'the faith', which may mean the prophet's own faith (prophesy as far as your faith reaches and no further) or the faith as a body of belief (prophecy must agree with it). The second reading gave rise to the theological phrase 'the analogy of faith'. Most recent interpreters prefer the first, in line with verse 3, but the question is not settled.

verse.text: if service, in the serving; if one teaches, in the teaching;
if one encourages, in the encouraging; the one who shares, with generosity; the one who leads, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.

note.traditional: he that ruleth; the one who leads

verse.note: The verb can mean to preside or lead, and also to care for or give aid, as a patron would. Because it stands here between sharing and showing mercy, some scholars prefer 'the one who gives aid'. The translation follows the more common reading.

verse.text: Let love be without pretense. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good.
In your love as brothers and sisters, be devoted to one another; in showing honor, outdo one another.
In diligence, do not be slack; in spirit, be fervent; serve the Lord.
verse.note: The verb means to boil or seethe. 'Spirit' may be the human spirit (be fervent inwardly) or the Holy Spirit (be set aglow by the Spirit); the Greek does not distinguish, and translations and commentators are divided.

verse.text: In hope, rejoice; in affliction, endure; in prayer, persist.
Share in the needs of the holy ones; pursue hospitality.
verse.note: The traditional 'saints' now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Paul uses the word of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. Many translations keep 'saints'; others use 'God's people'.

verse.text: Bless those who persecute; bless and do not curse.
verse.note: Many manuscripts read 'those who persecute you', as in the similar saying of Jesus. Some early witnesses lack 'you', and the Greek text translated here follows them. The sense is little affected.

verse.text: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.
Think the same way toward one another; do not think lofty thoughts, but go along with the lowly. Do not think yourselves wise.

note.traditional: men of low estate; the lowly

verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine (lowly people) or neuter (humble things, such as menial tasks). The contrast with 'lofty thoughts' favours the neuter, but the adjective elsewhere in the New Testament refers to people. The verb means to be carried along with something, hence 'go along with'.

verse.text: Repay no one evil for evil. Take thought for what is honorable in the sight of all people.
If possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.
Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for the wrath, for it is written: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay,” says the Lord.
verse.note: The Greek says only 'the wrath'; 'of God' is not in the text, though many translations add it. Almost all interpreters take it as God's judgment, as the quotation from Deuteronomy 32:35 that follows indicates. The point is to step aside and leave justice to God.

verse.text: On the contrary, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him a drink; for by doing this you will heap burning coals on his head.”

note.term: heap burning coals on his head
note.traditional: heap coals of fire on his head

verse.note: The verse quotes Proverbs 25:21–22 in its Greek form. The meaning of the image is disputed. Most interpreters take it as the burning shame or remorse that kindness awakens in an enemy and that may lead to a change of heart. Others take it as a sign of the judgment the enemy incurs by persisting. The next verse, about overcoming evil with good, favours the first.

verse.text: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.
Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been appointed by God.
verse.note: The Greek phrase, literally 'every soul', is a Septuagint idiom in which 'soul' simply means an individual human being. Older English versions kept 'soul', which now suggests an inner or immaterial part of a person. Most modern translations render it 'everyone' or 'every person'.

The phrase was ordinary language for civic and imperial officials, and the following verses (rulers, the sword, taxes) show that Paul means them. A minority of scholars have argued that angelic powers standing behind the state are also in view, but few accept this today. Verses 1 and 2 play on one Greek root, used for 'be subject', 'appointed', 'opposes' and 'what God has appointed'; English can keep only part of this.

verse.text: So whoever opposes the authority has resisted what God has appointed, and those who have resisted will bring judgment on themselves.
For rulers are not a cause of fear to good conduct but to evil. Do you want not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it,
for it is God's servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid, for it does not carry the sword for nothing. It is God's servant, an avenger bringing wrath on the one who practices evil.
verse.note: The words pick up 12:19, where believers are told not to avenge themselves but to leave room for 'the wrath', because vengeance belongs to God. Paul now presents the governing authority as one channel of that wrath, which is why verse 5 speaks of 'the wrath' with the article. The sword stands for the authority's power to punish by force; whether it refers specifically to capital punishment is debated.

verse.text: Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of the wrath but also because of conscience.
This is also why you pay taxes, for they are God's officials, devoting themselves to this very thing.
verse.note: The word denoted someone who performed a public service, and in the Septuagint it was also used of those serving in the temple. 'Ministers' now suggests clergy to most readers, so 'officials' is used. Whether Paul intends a sacred overtone here is uncertain. Most interpreters take the sense to be civic, with the genitive 'God's' supplying the theological point.

verse.text: Pay to all what is owed: tax to whom tax is owed, customs to whom customs, fear to whom fear, honor to whom honor.

note.term: tax to whom tax is owed, customs to whom customs
note.traditional: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom

verse.note: The first word refers to direct taxes or tribute levied on subject peoples, the second to indirect charges such as customs duties and tolls. The Roman historian Tacitus records public complaints about the collection of indirect taxes in Rome during the 50s, close to the time of this letter. The repeated 'owed' sets up the play on 'owe' in verse 8.

note.traditional: respect to whom respect is owed

verse.note: Many modern translations soften this to 'respect', while older versions have 'fear'. 'Fear' is kept because it is the same word used in verses 3 and 4, where it plainly means fear. Some interpreters, comparing 1 Peter 2:17, think the one owed fear is God and not the ruler; the Greek does not decide.

verse.text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves the other has fulfilled the law.

note.term: the one who loves the other has fulfilled the law
note.traditional: he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law

verse.note: The Greek could also be read 'the one who loves has fulfilled the other law', taking 'other' with 'law' (for example, the Mosaic law as distinct from civil obligations). Nearly all translators and commentators take 'the other' as the object of 'loves', meaning the other person, and that reading is followed here.

verse.text: For the commandments “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and any other commandment there is, are summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

note.traditional: Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness

verse.note: Many later manuscripts add 'You shall not bear false witness' after 'You shall not steal', and the King James Version includes it. The earliest witnesses lack it, and it is generally regarded as a scribal addition to fill out the list from the Ten Commandments. The final quotation is Leviticus 19:18.

verse.text: Love does no evil to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.
And do this knowing the time: it is already the hour for you to wake from sleep, for now our salvation is nearer than when we came to believe.
The night is far advanced, and the day has drawn near. So let us throw off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.
verse.note: Manuscripts divide between two verbs here: one meaning 'throw off' and one meaning 'lay aside' or 'take off', as with clothing. The SBLGNT prints the former; the other major critical edition prints the latter. The sense is little affected.

The Greek word covers military equipment in general and often means 'weapons', as it probably does in 2 Corinthians 6:7 and 10:4. 'Armor' is kept here because the verb is 'put on', the language of clothing that runs through verses 12 to 14. 'Weapons of light' is an equally possible rendering.

verse.text: Let us walk decently, as in the daytime: not in revelry and drunkenness, not in sleeping around and debauchery, not in strife and jealousy.
verse.note: The Greek word means 'bed' and, in the plural as here, is a euphemism for sexual encounters. 'Sexual immorality' is the usual English for a different and broader Greek word, so an English idiom that keeps the bed image and the plural sense is used instead. The word paired with it, rendered 'debauchery', denotes conduct without restraint or shame.

verse.text: Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh to gratify its desires.
Welcome the one who is weak in faith, but not in order to pass judgment on opinions.

note.term: not in order to pass judgment on opinions
note.traditional: not to quarrel over opinions; not to doubtful disputations

verse.note: The Greek phrase is compressed and can be read two ways. Many translations take it as 'not for quarrels over opinions'. The noun elsewhere in the New Testament means distinguishing or assessing, so it is rendered here as passing judgment, which also fits the chapter's repeated warnings against judging. The 'opinions' are the scruples or reasonings of the weak person.

verse.text: One person believes he may eat anything, but the one who is weak eats vegetables.
The one who eats must not look down on the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.
Who are you to judge someone else’s household slave? Before his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verse.note: The word denotes a domestic slave, a member of a household who answered to its master alone. Most translations have 'servant', which hides the point that an outsider had no standing to assess another owner's slave. 'Master' and 'the Lord' in this verse translate the same Greek word, and Paul plays on it: the slave's master turns out to be the Lord.

verse.text: One person judges one day above another; another judges every day alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind.

note.traditional: esteems / regards / considers one day above another

verse.note: The verb is the same one translated 'judge' throughout the chapter, here in its neutral sense of forming an assessment. Most translations vary the English to 'esteems' or 'considers'. 'Judges' is kept so that the reader can hear Paul's repetition of the word. The days in view are probably sabbaths and festivals of the Jewish calendar, though Paul does not say so.

verse.text: The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord. And the one who eats, eats for the Lord, for he gives thanks to God; and the one who does not eat, it is for the Lord that he does not eat, and he gives thanks to God.
For none of us lives for himself, and none dies for himself.
If we live, we live for the Lord, and if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.
For this is why Christ died and came to life: so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
But you, why do you judge your brother? Or you, why do you look down on your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God,
verse.note: Believers addressed and referred to one another as siblings, and the word here means any fellow member of the community, man or woman. The singular 'brother' is kept throughout the chapter because Paul is picturing one individual facing another.

note.traditional: the judgment seat of Christ (KJV); the judgment seat of God

verse.note: The word denotes the raised platform from which a magistrate heard cases, a familiar sight in any Roman city. The earliest manuscripts read 'of God'. Many later ones read 'of Christ', probably under the influence of 2 Corinthians 5:10.

verse.text: for it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will acknowledge God.”
verse.note: With this construction the verb in the Septuagint usually means to give open praise or acknowledgement, and it is so taken here. 'Confess to God' in the sense of admitting sins is possible and would suit the context of judgment. The quotation is Isaiah 45:23, introduced with the oath formula 'As I live, says the Lord', which occurs elsewhere in the prophets.

verse.text: So then, each of us will give an account of himself.

note.term: will give an account of himself
note.traditional: will give an account of himself to God

verse.note: Many manuscripts add 'to God' at the end of the verse, and most English translations include it. The SBLGNT text follows the witnesses that lack the words. The sense is the same either way, since the previous verses have already named God as judge.

verse.text: So let us no longer judge one another. Instead, let this be your judgment: never to put a stumbling block or a trap in a brother’s way.
verse.note: In the Septuagint and in period usage the word refers to a snare or something that trips a person up, and figuratively to whatever leads someone into ruin or sin. The traditional 'hindrance' is too mild. The related verb in verse 21 is rendered 'is made to fall'.

verse.text: I know and am convinced in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; only to the one who considers something unclean, to that person it is unclean.
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means 'common' or 'shared'. In Jewish usage it had come to mean ritually profane, unfit for those keeping the purity and food laws. That usage would have been clear to readers familiar with Jewish practice and puzzling to others. The issue in this chapter is food regarded as defiling, whether under the Mosaic food laws or through other scruples.

verse.text: For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not by your food destroy that person for whom Christ died.
So do not let this good of yours be slandered.

note.traditional: your good; what you regard as good

verse.note: Paul does not say what 'your good' is. Most interpreters take it as the freedom of the strong to eat anything, which would be spoken of as evil if it harmed others. Others take it as the good that the whole community shares, the gospel or its salvation, brought into disrepute among outsiders by the quarrel.

verse.text: For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.
Whoever serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by people.
So then, let us pursue what makes for peace and for building one another up.
Do not tear down the work of God for the sake of food. All things are clean, but it is bad for the person whose eating is a stumbling block.

note.term: whose eating is a stumbling block
note.traditional: who makes another stumble by what he eats; who eats with offence

verse.note: The Greek says literally 'who eats through a stumbling block'. It may refer to the strong person whose eating causes someone else to stumble, which is the more common view and fits verse 21. It may instead refer to the weak person who eats against his conscience and so stumbles. The rendering leaves both possibilities open.

verse.text: It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything by which your brother stumbles or is made to fall or is weak.

note.term: or is made to fall or is weak
note.traditional: stumbles (shorter text); stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak (KJV)

verse.note: Several early and important manuscripts end the verse at 'stumbles', and many modern translations follow them. The SBLGNT prints the longer reading, found in other early witnesses and in the majority of manuscripts, and it is translated here.

verse.text: The faith that you have, keep to yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves.
But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because it is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.
verse.note: The standard view, followed here, is that this form of the verb means to be divided in oneself, to waver or doubt. That sense is not clearly attested before the New Testament, where the form otherwise means to dispute or to make distinctions. A minority of scholars therefore read 'the one who disputes' or 'who makes distinctions'. The verb belongs to the same word-family as 'judge' and 'condemned' in verses 22 and 23, a play on words that English cannot reproduce.

verse.text: We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those who are not, and not please ourselves.
Each of us should please our neighbor for their good, to build them up.
For Christ also did not please himself; rather, as it is written: “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”
For whatever was written in earlier times was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.
May the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another, in keeping with Christ Jesus,
so that together, with one voice, you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you, to the glory of God.
For I say that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised for the sake of God’s truthfulness, to confirm the promises made to the fathers,
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘for the truth of God’. In the Greek Scriptures this word often describes God’s reliability in keeping his word, and the next clause, about confirming the promises, shows that this is the sense here. Several modern translations render it similarly.

verse.text: and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy, as it is written: “Therefore I will give thanks to you among the Gentiles, and sing to your name.”

note.term: and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy
note.traditional: and that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy

verse.note: The grammar linking this clause to verse 8 is disputed. It is taken here as a second purpose of Christ’s becoming a servant, alongside confirming the promises. It can also be read as a second thing Paul asserts: ‘I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcised... and that the Gentiles glorify God for mercy’.

The Greek word means ‘nations’ or ‘peoples’, and in the plural it was the ordinary Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples. The same word stands behind every ‘Gentiles’ in this chapter. In the Scriptures Paul quotes in verses 9–12 it could equally be rendered ‘nations’, and Paul’s argument depends on hearing it as the same word throughout.

verse.text: And again it says: “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.”
And again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples praise him.”
And again Isaiah says: “The root of Jesse will come, the one who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.”
verse.note: The quotation is Isaiah 11:10 in its Greek form. Jesse was the father of King David, so the phrase points to the expected king from David’s line. The verb translated ‘rises’ is also the ordinary word for rising from the dead, and Paul’s readers may have heard that overtone.

verse.text: May the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
I myself am convinced about you, my brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able also to admonish one another.
verse.note: The Greek plural is grammatically masculine but was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women. Paul is writing to the whole assembly, which chapter 16 shows included many women. Many modern translations render it this way, while others keep ‘brothers’.

verse.text: But I have written to you rather boldly on some points, by way of reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God
to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving the good news of God as a priest, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, made holy by the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘gospel’. The Greek word was an ordinary one for an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler’s accession, and the Greek version of Isaiah uses the related verb for the announcement of God’s reign. ‘Gospel’ is an old English word with the same meaning, but it now sounds like a religious technical term.

Paul describes his mission in the language of temple worship: ‘minister’, ‘serving as a priest’, ‘offering’, ‘acceptable’ and ‘made holy’ are all terms used of sacrifice. Most interpreters take the phrase to mean that the Gentiles themselves are the offering Paul presents to God. It can also mean the offering the Gentiles bring, which is their worship and obedience.

verse.text: In Christ Jesus, then, I have reason to boast about what relates to God;
for I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed,
by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit; so that from Jerusalem and around as far as Illyricum I have fully proclaimed the good news of Christ,
verse.note: The manuscripts differ here. Many, including some early ones, read ‘the Spirit of God’, and others read ‘the Holy Spirit’. The edition translated here prints the shortest reading, ‘the Spirit’, and the meaning is the same in each case.

verse.text: and in this way I make it my ambition to proclaim the good news not where Christ has already been named, so that I do not build on someone else’s foundation,
but as it is written: “Those who were never told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”
This is also why I have so often been hindered from coming to you.
But now, since I no longer have room in these regions, and since I have longed for many years to come to you
whenever I travel to Spain—for I hope to see you as I pass through and to be sent on my way there by you, once I have first enjoyed your company for a while—

note.traditional: whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you

verse.note: Paul’s sentence, begun in verse 23, breaks off here and is never completed. He interrupts himself to explain his hope and then turns to the Jerusalem journey. Later manuscripts add ‘I will come to you’ to repair the grammar, and many translations smooth the sentence in other ways. The break is left visible here.

verse.text: but now I am going to Jerusalem in service to the holy ones.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is ‘saints’, which now suggests canonised individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the language of the Greek Scriptures for Israel. Many translations keep ‘saints’, and others use ‘God’s people’.

verse.text: For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to share something of their own with the poor among the holy ones in Jerusalem.
They were pleased to, and indeed they are in their debt; for if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they owe it to them also to minister to them in material things.
So when I have completed this and have delivered this fruit to them under my seal, I will set out for Spain by way of you.

note.term: delivered this fruit to them under my seal

verse.note: Literally ‘having sealed this fruit to them’. The ‘fruit’ is the collection of money. The image is probably commercial: goods were sealed to guarantee that they arrived intact and to mark the transfer as complete, so the sense is that Paul will see the gift securely and formally handed over. The exact force of the idiom is uncertain.

verse.text: And I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of Christ’s blessing.
I urge you, brothers and sisters, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to strive together with me in your prayers to God on my behalf,
that I may be rescued from the disobedient in Judea, and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the holy ones,

note.traditional: unbelievers / those who do not believe

verse.note: Many translations have ‘unbelievers’. The Greek verb means to refuse to comply or be persuaded, and Paul uses it elsewhere in Romans for refusal of the good news, in contrast to the ‘obedience’ of verse 18. He is referring to people in Judea who reject the message about Christ, so in practice the two renderings point to the same group.

verse.text: so that by God’s will I may come to you in joy and find rest in your company.
May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is also a deacon of the assembly in Cenchreae,
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means someone who serves or carries out a task for another, and elsewhere in this translation it is 'servant'. Here it is tied to a particular assembly ('a deacon of the assembly in Cenchreae'), which suggests a recognised role, so 'deacon' is used. This is disputed: many translations have 'servant', and how formal such roles were at this early date is uncertain. The word is the same form used for men; 'deaconess' reflects a later, separate office.

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Greek Old Testament's term for Israel assembled before God. 'Church' is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution, neither of which existed. This translation uses 'assembly' wherever the word occurs.

verse.text: so that you may welcome her in the Lord in a way worthy of the holy ones and stand by her in whatever matter she may need you; for she herself has been a patron of many, and of me myself.
verse.note: The word is used of all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament's language for Israel. 'Saints', kept by many translations, now suggests canonised individuals or people of unusual virtue. Others render it 'God's people'.

The word is the feminine of a term for a patron, protector or presiding figure: someone of means and standing who used them on behalf of others. Older translations have 'helper', which undersells it; several recent ones have 'benefactor' or 'patron'. It echoes the verb just translated 'stand by': the Romans are to stand by her because she has stood up for many.

verse.text: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my co-workers in Christ Jesus,
who risked their own necks for my life; not only I but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles give thanks to them.
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary one for 'nations' or 'peoples'; in Jewish usage the plural meant the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it 'Gentiles' in that sense and 'nations' where peoples as such are meant. It is one Greek word throughout.

verse.text: Greet also the assembly that meets in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Asia for Christ.
verse.note: Asia here is the Roman province in the west of what is now Turkey, whose chief city was Ephesus, not the continent. 'Firstfruits' is a harvest image from Israel's offerings: Epaenetus was the first convert there, with the rest of the harvest to follow.

verse.text: Greet Mary, who has worked very hard for you.
Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kin and my fellow prisoners, who are outstanding among the apostles and who were in Christ before I was.
verse.note: The Greek form could in theory belong to a man's name, 'Junias', and many twentieth-century translations printed it that way. But no such male name has been found in ancient sources, whereas Junia was a common Latin woman's name, and early Christian commentators took her to be a woman. Most scholars now read Junia, probably the wife or sister of Andronicus.

The phrase can also be read 'well known to the apostles', which would leave Andronicus and Junia outside that group; some recent translations take it so. The majority of scholars, and the early Greek-speaking interpreters, read it as counting them among the apostles. 'Apostles' would then have its wider sense of commissioned emissaries, not the Twelve.

The word means a relative, but Paul uses it in Romans 9:3 for his fellow Jews as a whole. Since six people in this chapter are so described (also verses 11 and 21), most scholars think he means fellow Jews, not members of his family. 'Kin' leaves both readings open.

verse.text: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.
Greet Urbanus, our co-worker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
Greet Apelles, proven in Christ. Greet those from the household of Aristobulus.

note.term: those from the household of Aristobulus
note.traditional: those of the household of Aristobulus

verse.note: The Greek is literally 'those from among Aristobulus's people'. A wealthy household included slaves and freed slaves, and it is some of these who are greeted, not Aristobulus himself, who may not have been a believer or even still alive. The same applies to Narcissus in the next verse. Attempts to identify the two men with known figures in Rome are plausible but unproven.

verse.text: Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those from the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.
Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who work hard in the Lord. Greet the beloved Persis, who has worked very hard in the Lord.
Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who is mine as well.
Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers and sisters with them.
Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the holy ones with them.
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the assemblies of Christ greet you.
I urge you, brothers and sisters, to watch out for those who cause divisions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you learned; turn away from them.
For such people are slaves not to our Lord Christ but to their own belly, and by smooth talk and fine-sounding words they deceive the hearts of the unsuspecting.
verse.note: The verb belongs to the word group for slavery and means to be someone's slave, which is stronger than 'serve'. This translation keeps slave language distinct from the separate word group for service, the one behind 'deacon' in verse 1.

verse.text: For word of your obedience has reached everyone, so I rejoice over you; but I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil.
The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
Timothy, my co-worker, greets you, as do Lucius, Jason and Sosipater, my kin.
I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a secretary, and here the secretary adds his own greeting in the first person. 'In the Lord' may go with 'greet you', as translated, or with 'wrote down this letter'.

verse.text: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole assembly, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, as does our brother Quartus.
The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

note.term: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.

verse.note: This verse is absent from the earliest manuscripts and omitted by many modern editions and translations, which regard it as a repetition of the blessing in verse 20. The Greek edition translated here includes it, and does not include the doxology that most Bibles print as verses 25–27. That doxology appears at different places in different manuscripts (here, after 14:23, or after 15:33), and its originality is disputed.
